summary: This experimental document lists steps recursive resolvers and authoritative servers can take on their own to defend query privacy from passive monitors. An active attacker can defeat the protection, but it is simpler and less risky to deploy than stronger defenses. The goal is to speed up opportunistic encrypted transport between resolvers and authoritative servers.

plainLanguage.summary: You can start whispering to a friend without asking anyone. It won't stop a spy right next to you, but it stops people just passing by.

subtitle: Encrypt DNS queries between resolvers and authoritative servers without prior coordination.

tldr.problem: DNS queries between recursive resolvers and authoritative servers are typically sent in cleartext, allowing passive network monitors to observe which domains people are looking up, a significant privacy leak.
tldr.mechanism: This specification allows recursive resolvers and authoritative servers to independently and unilaterally attempt encrypted transport (DoT or DoQ) for their queries without coordination. If encrypted transport is available, it is used; if not, the resolver falls back to cleartext, ensuring queries never fail.
tldr.outcome: Opportunistic encryption protects against passive observers for most DNS queries between resolvers and authoritative servers, though it does not defend against active attackers. Early-stage deployment can now happen without waiting for ecosystem-wide coordination.

today: RFC 9539 is an Experimental specification published in February 2024. It represents an initial step toward widespread encrypted DNS for recursive-to-authoritative queries and is not yet a Standards Track specification. The IETF expects implementation and operational experience to inform whether this approach should be advanced or if stronger mechanisms are needed.

sections.title: The Privacy Problem in DNS
sections.content:
The Domain Name System translates domain names (like example.com) into IP addresses. Most DNS queries travel in cleartext over the network, meaning anyone observing the traffic can see which domains users are looking up. While the stub-to-recursive hop (from a user's device to their resolver) has encrypted options like DoH (DNS over HTTPS), the recursive-to-authoritative hop (from a resolver to an authoritative nameserver) is usually unencrypted.

This RFC proposes unilateral opportunistic encryption for the recursive-to-authoritative hop. Unilateral means resolvers and authoritative servers can enable it independently without waiting for coordination. Opportunistic means the system tries encryption if available but gracefully falls back to cleartext if encryption fails, ensuring query resolution never fails. This approach is simpler and less risky to deploy than schemes requiring authentication or coordination, while still providing protection against passive network monitors.
sections.plainLanguage: Talk softly if the other person understands whispers, but speak up if they don't hear you.

sections.title: Encryption without Coordination
sections.content:
Previous DNS privacy work focused on protecting stub-to-recursive traffic or required full authentication and coordination between all parties. This specification takes a different approach: recursive resolvers and authoritative servers can independently enable encrypted transport on port 853 using either DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoQ (DNS over QUIC).

The key innovation is a probing policy where resolvers remember which servers support encrypted transport and use those encrypted sessions when available. If a server doesn't support encryption or an encrypted connection fails, the resolver automatically falls back to port 53 (cleartext). This allows partial deployment: some servers can enable encryption while others remain cleartext, and resolvers will use whichever transport works. No coordination, signaling, or authentication is required to get started.
sections.plainLanguage: Try the quiet way first; if it doesn't work, speak normally. Both you and your friend can decide separately whether to whisper.

sections.title: How Recursive Resolvers Handle Queries
sections.content:
A recursive resolver implementing this specification maintains per-server state tracking which encrypted transports (DoT or DoQ) have worked recently. The resolver typically sends queries over Do53 (cleartext port 53), but remembers when a server recently succeeded with encrypted transport. If encrypted transport is remembered as working for a server, the resolver sends the next query over that encrypted transport instead, skipping cleartext entirely.

When sending queries on encrypted transport, the resolver should not include Server Name Indication (SNI) to avoid leaking which domain is being queried. Queries should be padded to mitigate traffic analysis. If an encrypted connection fails, the resolver falls back to cleartext for that server and waits a damping period (default 1 day) before retrying encryption. If encryption succeeds, the resolver remembers this for the persistence period (default 3 days) and continues using encrypted transport for subsequent queries to that server.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep a list of servers that take whispers. For others, shout. Remember for 3 days that someone accepts whispers.

sections.title: What Authoritative Servers Must Do
sections.content:
An authoritative server implementing this specification must enable either DoT or DoQ (or both) on port 853. The server can use a self-issued certificate (no need for a CA-signed certificate) and does not need to authenticate recursive clients. The responses returned over encrypted transport must contain the same data as responses over Do53, though response sizes may differ slightly due to transport characteristics.

Operators should be aware that encrypted connections from resolvers can consume server resources. Section 3.4 of RFC 7858 (for DoT) and Section 5.5 of RFC 9250 (for DoQ) provide guidance on managing connections. If resources are exhausted, servers can proactively close connections (preferring to close idle connections first) or decline new connections. In a pooled setup behind a load balancer, operators should ensure all pool members enable encryption simultaneously to avoid timeouts.
sections.plainLanguage: Start listening for whispers on the special door. Use any certificate. Close idle conversations if you run out of space.

sections.title: What This Protects and What It Doesn't
sections.content:
This specification protects against passive network monitors observing queries between resolvers and authoritative servers. However, it provides no defense against active attackers who can intercept and modify traffic. An active attacker can force a resolver to fall back to cleartext by blocking encrypted connections, or can act as a man-in-the-middle since the resolver accepts any certificate without verification.

To understand what is still required, resolvers and authoritative servers should implement additional privacy practices like QNAME minimization (RFC 9156) and local root zone caching (RFC 8806). Future work could add authentication and signaling mechanisms to defend against active attackers, but such mechanisms are out of scope for this opportunistic approach. This specification is explicitly designed as a stepping stone toward stronger defenses, not as a complete privacy solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Whispers stop someone listening from far away, but won't stop someone standing next to you. Other tricks are needed for that.

sections.title: Deployment Parameters and Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
Recursive resolvers following this specification set three system-wide parameters per encrypted transport: persistence (how long to remember a successful connection, default 3 days), damping (how long to remember a failed connection, default 1 day), and timeout (how long to wait for a connection to complete, default 4 seconds). Each parameter can be configured independently for DoT and DoQ.

The resolver maintains a per-server state table indexed by the authoritative server's IP address (not hostname), tracking whether encryption worked, when it was last tried, and maintaining session resumption tickets for faster reconnection. When multiple queries are in flight to the same server, the resolver should pipeline them over a single connection and be capable of receiving responses out of order. Implementers are encouraged to publish their chosen parameter values to help the community understand deployment patterns and assess the overall effectiveness of opportunistic encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Each resolver remembers for 3 days that a server whispers, then waits 1 day before trying if it stops. These numbers can be adjusted.
